question.leadin: He was killed near the end of a June 1876 battle in the Montana territory.
question.text: Name that 7th Cavalry commander famous for his "last stand."
question.clue: In one battle, this man decided not to wait for Alfred Terry's troops.

swap.text: This Republican won the Presidency in 1880 over Winfield Scott Hancock. Charles Guiteau shot him and he died in July 1881.
swap.clue: This man defeated Winfield Scott Hancock to become president, and the Pendleton Civil Service Act was passed after his death.

question.text: This women's rights advocate was not at Seneca Falls in 1848, though her parents and sister were there and signed the Declaration of Sentiments. In 1873, she was convicted and fined $100 -- a fine she refused to pay -- for voting while female.
question.clue: This woman is the alleged author of "Marriage and Maternity," an article published in The Revolution.

swap.text: At the ceremony, the Golden Spike was driven into the ground by this man, who at the time was president of the Central Pacific Railroad. Today, the spike is on display at the university he endowed.
swap.clue: In 1861, this man allied with Charles Huntington, Charles Crocker, and Mark Hopkins to create the Central Pacific Railroad, which met the Union Pacific at Promontory point.

question.text: This man was engaged in the "Erie War" with Jay Gould and Daniel Drew, and this railroad king had earlier worked for Gibbons' steamboat enterprise.
question.clue: During the California Gold Rush, this person created the Accessory Transit Company to bring passengers from the East Coast to San Francisco via Nicaragua.

swap.leadin: This speech states "Our war is not a war of conquest" and compares Cicero saving Rome from the Catiline conspiracy to Andrew Jackson saving America from the banks.
swap.text: Name this speech that describes a free silver convention in Memphis, and compares proponents of that platform to the Crusaders following Peter the Hermit.
swap.clue: This speech praises Thomas Benton's comparison of Andrew Jackson to Catiline, praising his actions "when he destroyed the bank conspiracy and saved America."

question.text: The Homestead steel works had been bought by this Scottish steel magnate who also wrote "The Gospel of Wealth" and founded a university in Pittsburgh.
question.clue: This person's employee Henry Frick called in the Pinkertons to brutally suppress the Homestead Strike.

swap.leadin: The Johnstown Flood occurred following the failure of the South Fork Dam owned by this founder of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club.
swap.text: Name this partner of Andrew Carnegie who locked out members of the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers from the Homestead Steel Works.
swap.clue: Joseph Duveen advised this man on purchasing works like Vermeer's Officer and Laughing Girl for his Fifth Avenue mansion.

question.text: Its main hope was to persuade Congress to authorize a vast program of public works, financed by a substantial increase of money in circulation, and to provide jobs. It came to an ignominious end when its leader was arrested for trespassing on lawns at the Capitol. For 15 points - name this "army" which left Massillon, Ohio in March of 1894 and marched to Washington, D.C.
question.clue: The wife of its leader gave birth to a son named Legal Tender.

swap.leadin: Secretary of the Treasury Abel Corbin attempted to end it by releasing some of the federal gold reserve.
swap.text: What was this September 24, 1869 event, the culmination of two speculators' attempt to corner the gold market, which drove the price up to $13.50 an ounce?
swap.clue: An important participant was Abel Corbin, who brought the architects of this scheme into high social circles.

question.leadin: Rural Free Delivery, or the right for people in remote agricultural areas to receive mail for free, was one political goal of this group, whose midsized conglomerates were named for Pomona, the Roman goddess of agricultural abundance.
question.text: Name this organization, established after Andrew Johnson commissioned Oliver Kelley to take a tour of the southern states. Founded in 1867, it remains the oldest active American agricultural advocacy group.
question.answerHtml: The Grange [accept The National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry; accept Grangers]
question.clue: This organization was formed in 1867 by Oliver Kelley to ensure the rights of farmers. It won a major victory on private warehouses in the court case Munn v. Illinois.

swap.leadin: As Governor, this man helped to take down the corrupt "Canal Ring."
swap.text: Name this man who earned his reputation battling Boss Tweed and Tammany Hall. He lost his most notable election thanks to a political compromise promising to remove federal troops from former Confederate states.
swap.clue: This man denied having sent the Cipher Dispatches and bequeathed four million dollars to a trust that helped establish the original New York City Public Library.

question.text: Chicago businessman Montgomery Ward, a competitor of this man, financed early Grange consumer cooperatives in the 1870s. After retiring, this man left his mail-order business to Julius Rosenwald.

swap.text: This industrialist, who was one of Field's collaborators in the Atlantic Telegraph Company, built an innovative steam locomotive called Tom Thumb for the B&O Railroad, and founded a namesake engineering and art school in Manhattan.
swap.clue: He obtained a patent for gelatin which he sold to Pearl Wait who invented the name Jell-O.

question.leadin: After being interviewed the night before by televangelist James Dobson, a man used one of these devices in 1989 in front of a crowd wearing Ronald Reagan masks and banging frying pans.
question.text: Name these devices that included one used by William Kemmler. Studies conducted by George Fell helped the dentist Alfred P. Southwick create these devices.
question.answerHtml: electric chairs (The first clue refers to Ted Bundy.)
question.clue: Harold Brown promoted this object to display the danger of technology developed by Westinghouse and Tesla.

swap.leadin: In 2005, Herbert Hovenkamp stated that "exclusionary conduct" and other vertical practices have been controversial in this field for the past century.
swap.text: Name this law that concerns maintaining market competition through regulation of companies.
swap.clue: MLB was granted an exemption from one of these laws, which was first successfully used against the Northern Securities Company.

question.leadin: Answer the following about women who spied for the Union during the American Civil War.
question.text: Sarah E. Edmonds joined the rolls of recipients of these things thanks to an exaggerated memoir of her wartime spying. Grover Cleveland vetoed many expansions of these things promoted by the Grand Army of the Republic.
question.answerHtml: pensions [or retirement funds or equivalents; or pensioners; accept veterans’ pensions, soldiers’ pensions, private pensions, or pension rolls; accept Dependent and Disability Pension Act; prompt on funds, funding, payment, financing, benefits, relief, or equivalents of any]

swap.text: One of White's late visions warned of the fall to pantheism of this Seventh-Day Adventist, who was disfellowshipped in 1907. This person collaborated with White to manage the Battle Creek Sanitarium.
swap.answerHtml: Dr. John Harvey Kellogg [or Dr. Kellogg; or John Kellogg; or John H. Kellogg]
swap.clue: This man who created a breakfast cereal called "Granula," whose blandness was intended to stop masturbation.

question.leadin: In the second half of the 19th century, it was nearly impossible to secure the Republican presidential nomination without an endorsement from this organization.
question.text: Name this fraternal organization for Union Civil War veterans that pushed for veterans' pensions during the 1880s and '90s.
question.clue: As this organization's leader, John A. Logan began its tradition of annual flower decorations in May and also became James Blaine's VP nominee.

swap.leadin: Name these Asian elephants of note in the 20th and 21st centuries.
swap.text: This poor elephant was brought from Southeast Asia to join Adam Forepaugh's circus, which fraudulently billed her as the first elephant born in America. She later died on Coney Island.
